speakerBio: Diabetologist who leads the trust's recurrent-DKA multidisciplinary clinic alongside psychology and social work, and campaigns for every DKA discharge to carry a documented precipitant and prevention plan.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is admitted in DKA for the fourth time in eighteen months. The metabolic emergency is corrected smoothly — fluids, insulin, potassium — and the plan is to discharge him in the morning "once eating." But nobody has asked why. Why this admission? Why the pattern? Is it an infection nobody looked for? A silent heart attack? Is he omitting his insulin — and if so, is it because he cannot afford it, cannot cope, or is frightened of hypos? Fixing the sugar without answering these questions guarantees he will be back. This final session is about everything around the crisis: the precipitant hunt, the special situations that change the rules, and the prevention that stops the revolving door.

1 · 🔎 The precipitant hunt — the 5 I's

Every hyperglycaemic emergency has a trigger, and correcting the metabolism without treating the trigger is half a job. A memorable framework is the 5 I's:

The 5 I'sWhat to look forAction
InfectionPneumonia, UTI, cellulitis, foot sepsis, gastroenteritis — the commonest precipitantExamine fully, cultures, CXR, urinalysis; treat early. (Note: WCC is often raised in DKA even without infection)
Infarction / IschaemiaMyocardial infarction (frequently silent/painless in diabetics), stroke, mesenteric ischaemiaECG + troponin in every older or high-risk patient — do not rely on chest pain
Insulin omission / non-adherenceMissed doses, running out, deliberate omission, pump failure — a leading cause, especially in recurrent DKAAsk directly and non-judgementally; explore why
Intercurrent illnessAny acute illness, surgery, pancreatitis, trauma — physiological stress raises counter-regulatory hormonesIdentify and manage the underlying illness
IatrogenicSteroids, SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA), thiazides, antipsychotics, checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapyReview the drug chart; hold the culprit where appropriate
Correcting the glucose is treating the symptom. Finding the precipitant is treating the disease — always ask "why now?"
⚠️ The painless MI

Myocardial infarction is a classic DKA/HHS precipitant and in people with diabetes it is frequently silent — autonomic neuropathy blunts the anginal warning. A hyperglycaemic emergency can be the presentation of an MI. Every older or vascular-risk patient in DKA/HHS needs an ECG and a troponin, regardless of whether they report chest pain.

2 · 🚱 Euglycaemic DKA and SGLT2 inhibitors

One of the most dangerous traps in modern diabetes care: euglycaemic DKA — a true ketoacidosis (acidotic, ketotic, unwell) with a blood glucose that is normal or only mildly raised (often < 14 mmol/L). Because the glucose looks reassuring, the diagnosis is missed. The commonest modern cause is the SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin).

The mechanism

  1. SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucose to be excreted in the urine (glycosuria), so the blood glucose stays low even as ketoacidosis develops.
  2. They also promote ketogenesis — via lower insulin levels, higher glucagon, and increased fatty-acid oxidation.
  3. Add a trigger (illness, fasting, surgery, dehydration, alcohol, low carbohydrate intake, insulin reduction) and the patient tips into ketoacidosis without the glucose alarm ever going off.
💡 Check ketones, not just glucose

In any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor — nauseated, breathless, acidotic, vomiting — check blood ketones and a venous gas even if the glucose is normal. A normal glucose does NOT exclude DKA in these patients. Euglycaemic DKA is treated like any DKA (fluids + fixed-rate insulin) but you must add glucose early because the starting sugar is low.

Sick-day and surgery rules for SGLT2 inhibitors

  • Sick-day rule: hold the SGLT2 inhibitor during any acute illness, particularly with dehydration, reduced oral intake, vomiting or infection — and check ketones.
  • Surgery / fasting rule: stop the SGLT2 inhibitor before surgery — guidance advises omitting it for at least the 3 days before major/elective surgery (i.e. on the day and the preceding days) and not restarting until the patient is eating, drinking and clinically well, because the perioperative fast is a potent trigger for euglycaemic DKA.
  • Counsel every patient started on one to hold it and seek help if acutely unwell.
SGLT2 inhibitor + unwell/fasting/surgery = hold the drug and check ketones. A normal glucose is not a clean bill of health.

3 · 🤰 DKA in pregnancy

DKA in pregnancy is an obstetric and medical emergency that behaves differently and carries a high risk to the fetus (fetal loss rates historically substantial):

  • It occurs at lower glucose levels than in the non-pregnant patient — pregnancy is a state of accelerated starvation and enhanced ketogenesis, so euglycaemic DKA is more common — a pregnant woman can be in DKA with a glucose barely above normal.
  • It develops faster and is less well tolerated.
  • The fetal risk is high — maternal acidosis and volume depletion compromise placental perfusion; the priority is prompt maternal resuscitation, which is the best fetal resuscitation.
  • Manage with the usual DKA principles but urgently, with early senior obstetric, diabetes and critical-care involvement, fetal monitoring, and a low threshold for checking ketones in any unwell pregnant woman with diabetes.
⚠️ Don't be reassured by the glucose in a pregnant woman

A pregnant woman with type 1 diabetes who is vomiting with a glucose of 12 can be in established DKA. Check ketones and a gas early and treat urgently — the window before fetal compromise is short.

4 · 📋 Sick-day rules — the education that prevents admissions

Most DKA admissions in established diabetes are preventable, and structured sick-day rules are the frontline. Every patient with type 1 diabetes (and insulin-treated type 2) should know them:

  • NEVER stop your insulin — even when not eating. Illness raises insulin requirements; the glucose may stay up even with poor intake. Stopping insulin is the single commonest route into DKA.
  • Check blood glucose more frequently (e.g. every 2–4 hours) when unwell.
  • Check blood (or urine) ketones when unwell or when glucose is persistently high, and know the action thresholds.
  • Stay hydrated — plenty of sugar-free fluids; take carbohydrate/sugary drinks if unable to eat and glucose is low.
  • Take correction doses of rapid-acting insulin for high glucose/ketones per an agreed plan.
  • Know when to seek help — persistent vomiting, rising ketones despite correction doses, ketones that won't clear, drowsiness, or inability to keep fluids down → contact the diabetes team or attend hospital.
💡 The four rules patients remember

Keep taking insulin · Check ketones · Stay hydrated · Know when to call. Four lines on a fridge magnet prevent more DKA than any inpatient protocol.

5 · 🔁 Recurrent DKA and 'brittle' diabetes

A subset of patients present repeatedly with DKA — the so-called "brittle" diabetic. It is tempting to label them non-compliant and move on. That is both wrong and dangerous: recurrent DKA carries a high mortality and almost always signals an unmet need. The near-universal proximate cause is insulin omission, and the job is to understand why:

  • Psychosocial and mental health drivers — depression, anxiety, eating disorders (including "diabulimia", deliberate insulin omission to lose weight), needle phobia, alcohol and substance misuse.
  • Socioeconomic drivers — deprivation, homelessness, inability to afford insulin or testing supplies, chaotic circumstances, poor access to care.
  • Knowledge and self-management gaps — never properly educated, or overwhelmed.

The intervention is not another lecture on carbohydrate counting; it is addressing the real driver: psychology and psychiatry input, eating-disorder services, social work, addiction services, a named diabetes specialist nurse, simplified regimens, and continuity of care. Treat the person, not just the pancreas.

Recurrent DKA is a social and psychological diagnosis wearing a metabolic mask. Ask why the insulin is being missed — and fix that.

6 · 🛡️ Prevention & structured education

Prevention is the highest-value intervention in diabetes emergency care. The evidence-based components:

  • Structured education programmes — e.g. DAFNE-type courses for type 1 — reduce severe hyper- and hypoglycaemic events and improve self-management.
  • Sick-day rule education delivered and revisited, not given once and forgotten.
  • Technology — continuous/flash glucose monitoring with alarms, insulin pumps with suspend features — for appropriate patients.
  • Access to the diabetes team — a helpline, rapid clinic review, and named specialist-nurse contact so patients call before they arrest, not after.
  • A post-DKA review before discharge: what precipitated it, was there a modifiable cause, is the education/technology/psychosocial support in place to stop the next one? Every DKA admission is a prevention opportunity.

7 · 🧮 Precipitants & special-situations summary

SituationKey pointAction
InfectionCommonest precipitantCulture, image, treat early; WCC unreliable in DKA
Silent MIOften painless in diabeticsECG + troponin routinely
SGLT2 inhibitorEuglycaemic DKAHold when unwell/fasting; stop ~3 days pre-surgery; check ketones despite normal glucose
PregnancyDKA at lower glucose, high fetal risk, fastUrgent; senior obstetric + diabetes + ICU; fetal monitoring
SteroidsRaise glucose & precipitate crisisAnticipate, monitor, adjust insulin
Recurrent DKAInsulin omission + psychosocial driverPsychology, eating-disorder & social support; DSN continuity

8 · 💀 M&M — the preventable revolving door

⚠️ Morbidity & Mortality: "we kept fixing the DKA and never asked why"

A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted with DKA for the sixth time in two years. Each admission followed the same pattern: rapid, competent correction of the metabolic emergency, a note that she was "non-compliant with insulin," and discharge within 48 hours. No admission had explored why she was omitting insulin. On this occasion she was found unconscious at home and could not be resuscitated; the coroner heard that she had a long-standing eating disorder and deliberately omitted insulin to control her weight (diabulimia), compounded by untreated depression and social isolation — none of it addressed across six admissions because the focus never moved beyond the sugar. The lesson is stark: recurrent DKA is a warning sign, not a nuisance. Each admission was a missed opportunity to engage mental-health, eating-disorder and diabetes-specialist services. Fixing the metabolism repeatedly while ignoring the driver is not treatment — it is a revolving door that ends, too often, in the mortuary.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Always hunt the precipitant — the 5 I's: Infection, Infarction/ischaemia, Insulin omission, Intercurrent illness, Iatrogenic. Ask "why now?"
  2. MI is often silent in diabetics — ECG and troponin in every older/high-risk patient regardless of chest pain.
  3. Euglycaemic DKA is real: SGLT2 inhibitors cause ketoacidosis with a normal glucose — check ketones, not just glucose, in any unwell patient on one.
  4. SGLT2 rules: hold when acutely unwell/fasting, stop ~3 days before surgery, restart only when eating and well.
  5. DKA in pregnancy occurs at lower glucose, develops fast, and carries high fetal risk — treat urgently with senior input.
  6. Sick-day rules: never stop insulin, check ketones, stay hydrated, know when to seek help.
  7. Recurrent/'brittle' DKA is driven by insulin omission — psychosocial, mental-health, eating-disorder and deprivation factors — address the real driver, not the pancreas.
  8. Prevention — structured education, technology, diabetes-team access and a post-DKA review — is the highest-value intervention. Every admission is a prevention opportunity.

moderatorQs.q: A 68-year-old with type 2 diabetes presents in HHS with no chest pain. Your registrar has 'no cardiac symptoms' documented and no ECG done. What is your concern?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: My concern is a silent myocardial infarction, which is both a classic precipitant of HHS and frequently painless in people with diabetes because autonomic neuropathy blunts the anginal warning — a hyperglycaemic emergency can be the presenting feature of an MI. 'No chest pain' is therefore not reassurance and must never substitute for objective testing. Every older or vascular-risk patient in DKA or HHS needs an ECG and a troponin as part of the routine precipitant screen, alongside a search for infection (the commonest trigger). Correcting the metabolic derangement flawlessly while missing an untreated MI is exactly the kind of omission that leads to a patient dying with perfectly normalised biochemistry. The 5 I's — Infection, Infarction, Insulin omission, Intercurrent illness, Iatrogenic — should be actively worked through in every case.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on dapagliflozin presents vomiting and breathless with a venous pH of 7.15, ketones of 4 mmol/L, but a glucose of only 11 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis and what are the two management points that differ from ordinary DKA?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is euglycaemic DKA caused by the SGLT2 inhibitor — a genuine ketoacidosis (acidotic, ketotic, unwell) with a near-normal glucose because the drug causes glycosuria and simultaneously promotes ketogenesis. The trap is that the reassuring glucose leads teams to miss the diagnosis, so the first principle is simply to check ketones and a gas despite the normal glucose. Two management points differ from ordinary DKA: first, you must add intravenous glucose early (alongside the fixed-rate insulin) because the starting sugar is low and the insulin needed to clear the ketones will drive it lower; and second, the SGLT2 inhibitor must be stopped and the patient counselled never to take it when acutely unwell or fasting. Otherwise it is treated as DKA with fluids and fixed-rate insulin.

moderatorQs.q: A young woman is admitted with DKA for the fifth time in two years and is labelled 'non-compliant'. Why is that label a clinical failure, and what should happen instead?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The label is a failure because it describes the behaviour and stops the enquiry exactly where it should begin. Recurrent DKA carries a high mortality and is almost always driven by insulin omission — but omission is a symptom, and the clinical task is to find its cause: psychosocial and mental-health drivers (depression, anxiety, needle phobia, and critically eating disorders such as diabulimia — omitting insulin to lose weight), socioeconomic factors (deprivation, inability to afford insulin or supplies, homelessness, chaos), or unaddressed education gaps. Instead of discharging with 'non-compliant,' she needs the real driver addressed: psychology/psychiatry, eating-disorder services, social work, a named diabetes specialist nurse, simplified regimens and continuity of care. Every recurrent admission is a warning sign and a missed prevention opportunity — treat the person, not just the pancreas.

audienceQs.q: What exactly should I tell a type 1 patient about managing their diabetes when they get a cold or a vomiting bug — the 'sick-day rules'?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The core message is never stop your insulin, even if you're not eating — illness raises your insulin needs and the glucose often stays high despite poor intake, so stopping insulin is the commonest way people end up in DKA. Beyond that: check your blood glucose more often (every 2–4 hours), check your ketones when unwell or when glucose is persistently high, stay well hydrated with sugar-free fluids (and take sugary fluids if you can't eat and your glucose is low), and take correction doses of rapid-acting insulin for high readings per your agreed plan. Crucially, know when to seek help — persistent vomiting, drowsiness, ketones that won't clear despite correction doses, or being unable to keep fluids down all mean contact the diabetes team or come to hospital. Four things patients remember: keep taking insulin, check ketones, stay hydrated, know when to call.

audienceQs.q: One of my pre-op patients is on empagliflozin. What do I need to do about it before their operation and why?
audienceQs.answerHTML: You need to stop the empagliflozin before surgery — guidance advises omitting SGLT2 inhibitors for around 3 days before major or elective surgery (i.e. on the day of surgery and the preceding days) and not restarting it until the patient is eating, drinking and clinically well postoperatively. The reason is euglycaemic DKA: the perioperative fast, dehydration and surgical stress are potent triggers for ketoacidosis in patients on these drugs, and because they keep the blood glucose low it can develop with a normal or only mildly raised glucose, so it is easily missed. If any patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor is unwell, vomiting, acidotic or breathless perioperatively, check blood ketones and a venous gas even if the glucose looks fine — a normal glucose does not exclude DKA.

audienceQs.q: For our patients who keep coming back with DKA, what actually reduces the readmissions?
audienceQs.answerHTML: What works is moving the focus from the metabolism to the reason the insulin is being missed. That means a proper multidisciplinary approach: access to psychology and psychiatry (for depression, anxiety, needle phobia and especially eating disorders/diabulimia), eating-disorder services, social work for deprivation, housing and affordability issues, and addiction services where relevant — because deprivation and psychosocial distress are the usual real drivers. Alongside that, continuity with a named diabetes specialist nurse, simplified insulin regimens, appropriate technology (flash/continuous glucose monitoring with alarms), structured education that is revisited rather than given once, and an easy-access helpline so they call before they crash. Every admission should trigger a documented review of the precipitant and a prevention plan before discharge — the readmissions fall when the underlying driver is addressed, not the sugar alone.
